title: Quiz 4 – Tail Recursion, Binary Search, and Runtime (log n vs n²)
notes: Tail recursion: the recursive call is the final action; enables optimization equivalent to iteration in some languages/compilers.
Converting tail recursion to iteration: carry accumulators as parameters.
Binary search on a sorted array halves the search space each step → Θ(log n) comparisons worst case.
Linear vs binary search: Θ(n) vs Θ(log n) on sorted input.
Quadratic runtimes (Θ(n²)) arise from double-nested loops (e.g., naive pair comparisons, insertion sort worst case).
Recurrence for binary search: T(n)=T(n/2)+Θ(1) ⇒ Θ(log n).

flashcards.back: A form of recursion where the recursive call is the last operation in the function.

flashcards.front: Why can tail recursion be optimized?
flashcards.back: No remaining work after the call, so the stack frame can be reused (TCO) when supported.
Use a loop with an accumulator multiplying 1..n.
Input must be sorted (or monotone predicate over index range).

flashcards.front: Give an example algorithm with Θ(n²) runtime.
flashcards.back: Bubble sort / selection sort / insertion sort (worst case).

flashcards.front: Space cost of recursive binary search.
flashcards.back: Θ(log n) call stack; iterative version uses Θ(1) space.
Tail-recursive factorial vs non-tail-recursive naive Fibonacci.
